app.title: Immune cell population composition and responder comparison dashboard
app.summary: On first load the dashboard builds a database from the trial's cell-count file, linking each sample to its subject and treatment. The person reads each sample's immune cell populations as percentages of its total count, either for every sample or for one picked sample, alongside the average composition across all samples. They then choose a cohort by condition, treatment and sample type, and compare responders with non-responders using box plots and a per-population table of rank tests, effect sizes and FDR-adjusted p-values. A fixed baseline subset is broken down by project, response and sex, and the frequency table, the comparison and the baseline sample list can each be downloaded as CSV.

task.text: Work out each sample's cell population composition and test whether any population differs between treatment responders and non-responders in a chosen cohort.

data.text: A table of samples. Each sample has raw counts for a fixed panel of cell populations and is linked to attributes of the subject (project, condition, age, sex) and of the sample (treatment, response, sample type, time from treatment start).
data.item: a blood sample from a trial subject, with a count for each cell population

stage.text: analysing trial cell counts to compare treatment responders with non-responders, before reporting

mechanism.text: Four tabs share one joined table of samples with per-sample percentages. A frequency table and a mean-composition bar chart give an overview, and three cascading selects narrow the data to a cohort. That cohort drives grouped box plots and a statistics table recomputed from it, and a fixed baseline subset is summarized as metrics and count tables. Each result table has its own CSV download.

field.text: immune cell population frequencies compared between treatment responders and non-responders in a clinical trial

workflow.name: compare a measured composition between two outcome groups within a chosen cohort

steps.here: if the database is missing, it is built from the cell-count CSV on first load, and the cell counts are joined to the sample and subject tables

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: each population's count becomes a percentage of that sample's total; the table can be narrowed to one sample, and a bar chart shows the mean percentage for each population across all samples

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: cascading selects for condition, then treatment, then sample type, each offering only the values that remain and defaulting to the study's main cohort; only samples with a yes or no response are kept
box plots of percentage for each population, coloured by responder versus non-responder, with outliers shown as points

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: for each population: medians and means for both groups, a Mann-Whitney U test, Welch's t-test, the rank-biserial effect size, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted p-values with a significance flag at 0.05
metrics and count tables for baseline (time 0) samples in one cohort, broken down by project, response and sex, plus the average count of one population for a defined subgroup
separate CSV downloads for the frequency table, the responder comparison and the baseline sample list

distinctive: counts are turned into relative frequencies within each sample, so the comparison is about composition, not absolute abundance
several populations are tested at once, so p-values are corrected with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate
an effect size (rank-biserial r) is shown next to each p-value, so that tiny differences reaching significance in large groups are not over-read
the cohort filters cascade: each select offers only the values that exist under the choices made above it
baseline is defined by time from treatment start being zero, and the breakdown counts unique subjects as well as samples
